 Trump’s attempt to discourage naturalized citizen voting backfired
 News Jeff Brumley  |  November 18, 2026
 Federal attempts to discourage naturalized citizens from voting in the midterm elections backfired on the Trump administration, according to a newly released exit poll.
 The survey found 53% of naturalized Americans who voted were extra-motivated to cast ballots because of the Trump administration’s tactics , including home interrogations by armed agents and attempts to deny their voting eligibility.
 The situation also drove them to be more intentional about how they voted, whether it was voting early, through absentee ballot or by taking a family member or friend with them to the polls, according to survey conducted by the U.S. Immigration Policy Center at the University of California at San Diego and the National Partnership for New Americans.
 Nicole Melaku
 “In the end, fear did not win,” said Nicole Melaku , executive director of NPNA. “Instead, naturalized voters chose hope, focused on their loved ones and made a plan to exercise their constitutionally protected right to vote.”
 Naturalized citizens showed resilience before and on Election Day, said Tom Wong , director of the U.S. Immigration Policy Center at UC San Diego.
 “Not only were they not deterred from voting, but they contributed to the record early voting numbers that we saw across the country and cemented themselves as an indispensable component of the new blue wall that has resulted,” Wong said.
 Immigration was a major concern for many of the demographic just as it was for Hispanics and other Americans. More than 78% of Americans said President Donald Trump’s detention and deportation campaign has “gone too far,” compared to 16% who said its “about right” and 4% who said it has “not gone far enough.”
 Over 78% either strongly or somewhat opposed enforcement actions at sensitive locations such as churches, hospitals and schools, while 82% opposed expanded efforts to revoke citizenship from naturalized Americans.
 Vanessa Cardenas
 Naturalized citizens “want leaders who recognize the contributions of immigrants rather than dehumanizing them,” said Vanessa Cardenas , executive director of America’s Voice. The lesson from this election is clear: Americans want solutions, not cruelty. They want their elected officials to make their lives better, not more expensive.”
 Economic issues were another major concern to naturalized citizen voters. The survey reported 78% considered grocery and food prices either extremely or very important. More than 14% said the issue was somewhat important.
 More than 74% cited housing costs, including mortgages and rents, as extremely or very important, while about 17% said those costs were somewhat important.
 Insurance, prescription drugs and other health care costs were considered extremely or very important by three quarters of naturalized citizen voters, and about 16% described those issues as somewhat important.
 Also, 69% of those surveyed identified jobs and wages as extremely or very important, and 20% said jobs and wages were somewhat important. Close to 70% blamed Trump’s policies for existing prices.
 Pollsters also reported Democrats’ edge with naturalized citizens rebounded from +4 points over Republicans in 2024 to +30 this year — further even than the +26 in the 2022 midterms.
 It’s clear from the survey and election results that naturalized Americans want to participate in democracy, said Angelica Salas , executive director of the Coalition for Humane Immigration Rights. “Throughout the year, and especially during the crucial months leading to the midterm elections, our members told us they would not be lied to, intimidated or silenced.”
